      Notes

      Copy the table. It is your reference for the rest of the unit.

      I. The seven laws, in one place

      LawRuleExample
      Product of powersam · an = am+n23 · 21 = 24
      Quotient of powersam ÷ an = am-n(−3)7 ÷ (−3)2 = (−3)5
      Power of a product(ab)m = am · bm(−7 · 3)2 = (−7)2 · 32
      Power of a quotient(a ÷ b)m = am ÷ bm(13 ÷ 5)3 = 133 ÷ 53
      Power of a power(am)n = amn(63)4 = 612
      Identity exponenta1 = a151 = 15
      Zero exponenta0 = 11270 = 1
      Grade 7 Accelerated · Unit 3 · Lesson 3 — Exponential Expressions4

      Notes

      Two students, two orders, one value.

      II. More than one law — make a plan, then follow it

      Winston:

      Yvette:

      1. Different plans, same value. Any correct sequence of laws gives the same answer.
      Grade 7 Accelerated · Unit 3 · Lesson 3 — Exponential Expressions5

      Notes

      III. Order of operations still applies

      1. Parentheses first — including a fraction bar, which is a pair of parentheses in disguise.
      2. Exponents next — the laws of exponents are applied here.
      3. Then multiply and divide, left to right; then add and subtract.
      4. Never across a + or a −: , not .

      Yesterday the exponent laws finished — numbers and letters.

      Today they go to work on twenty-digit numbers.

      Notes

      Copy the table.

      I. Powers of ten name the places

      101102103104105106

      1. The exponent counts the zeros — and names the place of the 1.
      Grade 7 Accelerated · Unit 3 · Lesson 8 — Writing Large Numbers in Scientific Notation4

      Notes

      II. Scientific notation

      with

      1. The coefficient is at least 1 and less than 10: one nonzero digit before the decimal point.
      2. The exponent is how many places the decimal point moves: 26,000,000. → 2.6, seven places, so 107.

      Notes

      III. How many times larger?

      1. Divide the coefficients. Divide the powers of 10. Multiply the two results.
      2. On a screen, 8.4E6 means 8.4 × 106.

      Writing Small Numbers in Scientific Notation

      MA.8.NSO.1.4

      I can write very small numbers in scientific notation, read them back, and find how many times larger or smaller one number is than another.

      Yesterday the exponents on the 10 were positive.

      Today they are negative — and the numbers get very small.

      Grade 7 Accelerated · Unit 3 · Lesson 9 — Writing Small Numbers in Scientific Notation1

      Warm-Up

      On your own. Four minutes. No notes.

      1.Write 4,300,000 in scientific notation.

      2.Write as a fraction.

      3. is between which two whole numbers?

      4.Write 0.007 as a fraction.

      Grade 7 Accelerated · Unit 3 · Lesson 9 — Writing Small Numbers in Scientific Notation2

      Warm-Up

      Answers.

      1.Write 4,300,000 in scientific notation.4.3 × 106

      2.Write as a fraction.

      3. is between which two whole numbers?9 and 10

      4.Write 0.007 as a fraction.

      Grade 7 Accelerated · Unit 3 · Lesson 9 — Writing Small Numbers in Scientific Notation3

      Notes

      Copy the table.

      I. Negative powers of ten name the decimal places

      10010-110-210-310-410-5
      10.10.010.0010.00010.00001

      1. A negative exponent puts the 1 in that decimal place: 10-4 is a 1 in the fourth place.
      Grade 7 Accelerated · Unit 3 · Lesson 9 — Writing Small Numbers in Scientific Notation4

      Notes

      II. Small numbers in scientific notation

      1. The coefficient is still at least 1 and less than 10. The exponent is negative for a number less than 1.
      2. The exponent is how many places the point moves: 0.0000672 → 6.72 is five places right, so 10-5.
      Grade 7 Accelerated · Unit 3 · Lesson 9 — Writing Small Numbers in Scientific Notation5

      Notes

      III. How many times larger — or smaller?

      1. Divide the coefficients. Divide the powers of 10 — subtract the exponents. Multiply the results.
      2. Which is bigger, 10-5 or 10-8? The one with the larger exponent: −5 > −8, so 10-5.
      Grade 7 Accelerated · Unit 3 · Lesson 9 — Writing Small Numbers in Scientific Notation6
